history.question: whats oops?
history.answer: Object-Oriented Programming in C# is a paradigm built on four core pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, and polymorphism, which we use to structure enterprise codebases around real-world business domains. In our production applications, we rely heavily on interfaces for abstraction and dependency injection to decouple services, making our systems highly maintainable and testable. Polymorphism allows us to write extensible business logic where services can process different implementations interchangeably through base interfaces without knowing their concrete types.

history.question: What is obstruction
history.answer: Abstraction in C# is the principle of hiding complex implementation details and exposing only the essential features of an object through abstract classes and interfaces. In our enterprise applications, we heavily rely on interfaces to define contracts for our services, which allows us to decouple our business logic from underlying data access or third-party integrations. This not only makes our codebase much easier to maintain and test, but it also enforces a clear boundary between components, enabling seamless dependency injection across our application architecture.

history.question: What is the difference between polymorphism
history.answer: In C#, polymorphism allows objects of different derived classes to be treated through a common base class interface. We primarily implement this using compile-time overloading and run-time overriding with virtual and override keywords. In our enterprise applications, this enables us to write extensible service layers where a single caller can execute distinct business logic behaviors seamlessly based on the instantiated runtime type.

history.question: What is SOLID principles
history.answer: In our enterprise C# codebases, we strictly adhere to the SOLID principles to maintain high modularity, testability, and maintainability. Single Responsibility ensures each class handles one distinct domain concern, while Open/Closed allows us to extend functionality via interfaces without modifying tested code. Liskov Substitution guarantees that derived classes like specific repository implementations can seamlessly replace their base abstractions. Interface Segregation keeps our contracts lean by preventing fat interfaces, and Dependency Inversion relies heavily on constructor injection through our native IoC container to decouple high-level services from low-level infrastructure.
